items.original_title: The EU is showing how regional maritime rules can support a global framework at the IMO
items.summary: In April 2025, governments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed on a historic global regulation, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way. Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan. While T&E analysis has previously shown that the NZF in itself is not strong enough to reduce shipping emissions at the pace countries agreed to, the agreement set an important global standard for a sector so far exempt from most climate rules. The EU is clear that if the IMO establishes a carbon pricing scheme such as the NZF, a ship sailing internationally will not have to pay double for the same emissions under the EU ETS. The newly proposed “ETS as a service” would allow EU trade partners to raise revenues on their own 50% shares through the EU’s existing system, without the administrative burden of setting up their own ETS from scratch. Now, the EU is opening a path for its regional rules to co-exist with a global framework and involving others in the benefits.

This is why I find the tendency to reduce training when companies come under financial pressure so short-sighted. Lifelong learning cannot be a phrase we use in speeches while treating the training budget as expendable when margins tighten. items.title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.original_title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.summary: Deployed capacity on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades during this year’s Golden Week holiday was the highest on record, according to new analysis from Sea-Intelligence. Port congestion in Asia, caused by a succession of typhoons, led to vessel bunching at loading ports, and subsequently resulted in a series of “double sailings”, which cancelled out carriers’ blanking strategy during the holiday period when they typically look to skip voyages due to a lack of cargo sitting on Asia’s docks “Double sailings are essentially two departures on a liner service in a week,” analysts at Sea-Intelligence said. “Liner services work on weekly departure frequencies – ie, one vessel departs the origin region every week. “When vessels get delayed, they bunch up – the delayed departure that moved from week 1 to week 2 is now sailing along with the original week 2 departure, hence a ‘double sailing’,” the consultancy explained. This meant deployed capacity during the Golden Week period – which Sea-Intelligence defined as taking place between weeks 40 and 42, to account for the lag in inland transport work unable to take place because drivers were on holiday – was this year higher on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades than ever before.

That programme will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, providing 288 Panamax slots alongside 270 neopanamax slots through competitive allocations in November. items.title: EU Proposed SMAP subsidy favors e-fuels and bioLNG
items.original_title: EU Proposed SMAP subsidy favors e-fuels and bioLNG
items.summary: Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. In July, the European Commission proposed a revision of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) that would reserve up to 110 million allowances between 2028 and 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which is meant to cover part of the price gap between fossil marine fuels and sustainable alternatives. Rystad Energy’s analysis shows that, combined with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would reshape the cost ranking of marine fuels in Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels stand to gain the most, while biodiesel made from used cooking oil (UCO) and animal fats – one of today’s most widely used marine biofuels – is left out. SMAP would cover 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with 10 additional percentage points where the feedstock is sourced in the EU. At 3Q26 prices, bioLNG costs more than twice as much as VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at about half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are counted.

items.summary: For years, shippers viewed the world in black and white: you either paid for Air (fast and expensive), or you settled for Ocean (slow and cheap). Here is how to choose the right transport mode for your freight needs with confidence. The Lens: Four factors to consider when choosing a freight mode Before committing to a lane, top-performing supply chains run their cargo through four strategic lenses. This ensures that the chosen mode is not merely a habit or reflex, but a calculated decision to protect the bottom line. The scenarios: When to choose air, ocean or sea-air freight This is where mode selection becomes practical. items.title: Trump Administration Unveils Seafood Strategy to Boost U.S. Fishing Fleet and Domestic Production
items.original_title: Trump Administration Unveils Seafood Strategy to Boost U.S. Fishing Fleet and Domestic Production
items.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry.

items.summary: The US waiver on Russian crude has reduced uncertainty for Indian and Chinese refiners, giving them greater confidence to continue purchasing economically attractive Russian grades while keeping alternative supply options open in case the situation changes, analysts and industry sources said Oct. 22. Despite fluctuations, China’s Russian crude intake averaged about 2.35 million b/d over January-September, GAC data showed, underscoring sustained demand for discounted Russian barrels. Tariffs on China’s Russian oil purchases could reignite trade tensions with the US while doing little to deter such purchases, given the economic appeal of discounted Russian crude for Chinese refiners.

items.title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
items.original_title: Sanctions risks reshape commodity trading
items.summary: In the briefing, authors Daniel Martin, HFW partner, and Amanda Rathbone, HFW knowledge counsel (commodities) said that sanctions compliance has evolved from a specialist legal consideration into a central strategic concern for commodity businesses trading oil, gas, metals and agricultural products. Martin and Rathbone warn that the sanctions environment is changing so rapidly that risks can evolve significantly during the lifecycle of a single transaction, from initial negotiations through to shipment, financing and payment. As a result, companies are increasingly being forced to reassess traditional compliance processes and adopt broader, more dynamic risk management strategies. Governments are increasingly using sanctions as instruments of broader geopolitical policy, meaning that ordinary commercial activity and seemingly routine commodity trades can now attract scrutiny. HFW warns that efforts to comply with one jurisdiction’s sanctions requirements can sometimes increase exposure to conflicting regulations elsewhere, creating difficult commercial and legal dilemmas for international trading businesses. The briefing also points to increasing expectations from regulators, who now expect companies to investigate broader sanctions risks throughout a transaction rather than relying solely on screening immediate contractual counterparties against sanctions lists. Martin and Rathbone believe sanctions complexity is unlikely to diminish.

items.original_title: Seafarers face widening competency gap as digital shipping accelerates, recent research finds
items.summary: Eighty two per cent of maritime professionals surveyed say current training does not adequately prepare crews for the realities of modern, digitally-enabled vessel operations. Just 18% believe training keeps pace, according to new research from OneOcean and Thetius. Seafarer training is falling behind rapidly evolving operational realities at sea, according to two new reports commissioned by OneOcean and conducted by maritime innovation consultancy Thetius. Findings reveal two interconnected challenges – that seafarers work in increasingly complex digital environments, and that maritime professionals do not feel well prepared to keep pace with this change. Alex Mangan, Chief Marketing and Communications Officer, OneOcean, said: “Change in shipping will only accelerate as vessels adopt new digital systems to manage tightening international regulation and to sail more efficiently and productively. “This has created a growing gap between the training seafarers receive and the challenges they face at sea. Closing this reality gap requires the industry to shift its approaches to competence, to reflect real-world operations.” Nick Chubb, Founder of Thetius, said: “The findings reveal a clear reality gap between the demands of modern shipping and the way competence is developed. As vessels become more digitally complex, the industry must move beyond compliance-based training and equip seafarers with the skills they need to operate safely and effectively.” OneOcean’s own product suite reflects this thinking.

REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels.

items.title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
items.original_title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
items.summary: By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million. Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said.

items.summary: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three years. The Vietnamese-flagged PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), reportedly carrying 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, departed St. Petersburg on October 15 and is currently signaling Norfolk as its destination, according to VesselFinder . The arrival would come five days ahead of another Russian diesel shipment identified by Reuters on Friday as the first cargo heading to the United States under a recent agreement between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The tanker has signaled New York as its destination, with an expected arrival date of November 7, although its final discharge port has not been confirmed. The two shipments come as the Trump administration moves to ease restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On October 9, Trump announced an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.

items.summary: European wholesale natural gas prices surged on Friday, on course to cap the week at their highest levels since late 2022, as an escalation in Middle East military conflict and diplomatic evacuations intensified anxieties over global LNG supply continuity ahead of winter. The benchmark rose 3.8% on Friday to trade at 93.40 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), locking in a weekly gain of nearly 7%. In Great Britain, the equivalent similarly advanced 3.5% to 229.00 pence per therm, on course to finish the week 6.2% higher. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis launched coordinated drone and missile strikes targeting civilian transport and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including a fatal strike on a civilian airport in Dammam and an attack on ’s Shaybah oilfield. The escalating conflict has severely restricted Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) carrier navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, forcing extended reroutings around Africa and drastically curtailing spot arrivals at European regasification terminals. Benchmark jumped to $114 per barrel on Friday – their highest level in over five months – reinforcing broad-based inflation and input cost pressures across energy-intensive European industries. The weekly surge across European gas curves leaves the continent acutely vulnerable as winter heating demand accelerates.

items.title: Singapore must look beyond the box to secure its logistics future
items.original_title: Singapore must look beyond the box to secure its logistics future
items.summary: Dropping behind Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan in the global container port rankings, and seeing Malaysia’s Port Klang and Port of Tanjung Pelepas nip at its heels should serve as a wake-up call for Singapore, in a changing competitive landscape for box trades For Singapore, this is about more than losing a place in a league table. It is an existential question asking whether a nation built on maritime trade can adapt to a world where supply chain control matters as much as moving containers. As Singapore spent years living off its geographical advantages, deepwater harbour and reputation for efficiency to guarantee continued dominance, its competitors have expanded their infrastructure, attracted manufacturing investment, and developed integrated logistics ecosystems. Part of the problem for Singapore with its nearest rival is that it simply cannot compete with Malaysia when it comes to land availability, meaning it should not focus on warehouses and distribution centres. And the pending Tuas Port, with its planned capacity of 65m teu on full completion in the 2040s, will have a part to play, even if success cannot be judged by volume alone. Yes, the Ministry of Transport’s new Connectivity & Logistics division recognises the need to integrate maritime, aviation, and land transport, but creating a coordinating body will not automatically deliver the commercial agility needed to compete.

items.title: NSR vs Suez: the Arctic is not a tradelane, it’s a corridor with a hefty premium
items.original_title: NSR vs Suez: the Arctic is not a tradelane, it’s a corridor with a hefty premium
items.summary: On 19 October, data from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) showed 104 ships had crossed Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) by 30 September, already more than in all of 2025. Four days earlier, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that containerships moved 2.19m teu through the Suez Canal last month, the most since the Houthi campaign began, and Linerlytica expects carriers to be fully back to Suez by the first quarter of 2027. Most coverage reads the first as proof that the Arctic is finally opening, but read together, they say something else: the part of the NSR Moscow planned and paid for has missed its targets by a wide margin, while the part it barely planned for has beaten them, because other people’s chokepoints closed. It isn’t that the NSR is missing from an Arctic section; the Arctic silk road itself is absent. Whatever the final figure, it is clear the season moved less than one 24,000 teu ship carries on a single Suez sailing. I costed the loop the way a carrier’s network team would: a 4,900 teu ship, eight seasonal sailings, west through the Arctic and back via Suez. The escort adds $150,000-$280,000 a transit, and Chinese sources put Arctic hull and P&I cover at three to five times normal rates.

items.original_title: South Korean Shipowner Sinokor Dominates Hormuz Transits as Oil Flows Rebound
items.summary: Oct 23, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined. Ships owned by Sinokor Group carried 105.6 million barrels of crude through the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets, an analysis of ship-tracking and other data from intelligence firms Vortexa, Equasis and Signal Group showed. That’s equivalent to almost 40% of oil making the crossing last month. of Saudi Arabia, also known as Bahri, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping unit — accounted for a combined 97.3 million barrels during the same period, according to Bloomberg calculations based on that data. When Hormuz was all but closed off, those tankers were snapped up at exorbitant rates by producers who needed to load oil or risk running out of storage space and then being forced to undertake costly shutdowns. As Gulf crude exports recover to close to pre-war levels, Sinokor is still among the most active owners in the so-called shuttling trade, with its vessels taking short trips to pick up oil from inside the Persian Gulf, sail through Hormuz and then discharge at ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman.

It is equipped with Everllence’s first commercial ammonia dual-fuelled two-stroke marine engine, which successfully completed factory acceptance testing in April 2026. The vessel is the result of a collaboration initiated in June 2022 by MPA, EPS, HHI, and the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) to develop an ammonia dual-fuelled gas carrier under the Singapore flag. As Singapore’s flag administration, MPA has worked closely with EPS, HHI, ABS, and other industry partners on the vessel’s technical and regulatory compliance. This included reviewing the vessel’s design against relevant International Maritime Organization (IMO) guidelines, participating in hazard identification and operability studies, and providing regulatory guidance on ammonia detection, fuel system safety, and emissions management. MPA also shared its experience from earlier ammonia trials to support the development of onboard safety procedures and crew preparedness.

items.original_title: Diesel arbitrage: why freight has shut the Europe import window

Red arbitrages do not stop diesel moving Refiners keep running because they earn the crack, and the diesel has to go somewhere. The flow data supports the point: • India to Europe diesel flows were suppressed from March to June, when the economics pointed east. The supply picture is a Russia and US story, not only a Middle East story The US Gulf Coast supplied almost half of North West Europe’s diesel imports over the past 12 months, a much larger share than a year earlier. The reductions were achieved through the use of liquefied biomethane (LBM) across eight international shipping voyages under 17 contracts between Hapag-Lloyd and ZEMBA members. The German container liner secured ZEMBA’s inaugural tender to replace conventional bunker fuels with lower-emission alternatives. It then allocated environmental attribute certificates representing the emissions reductions achieved during these voyages to ZEMBA members through a book-and-claim mechanism. ZEMBA members include major cargo owners such as Amazon, Nike, IKEA and Patagonia. Second tender moves to e-fuels ZEMBA has awarded its second tender to Hapag-Lloyd and Norwegian shipping company North Sea Container Line (NCL), with fuel deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027. Hapag-Lloyd will use e-methanol on a trans-oceanic trade route, while NCL will deploy green ammonia on a northern European route. Both fuels will be produced using green hydrogen generated with renewable energy and are expected to deliver lifecycle emissions reductions of at least 90% compared with conventional marine fuels. ZEMBA expects the two companies to collectively deliver around 120,000 mtCO2e in emissions reductions over three years from 2027.

items.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. items.summary: Sierra Leone has launched a new national shipping company backed by China’s Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with ambitions to develop a fleet of 50 vessels and capture a greater share of the country’s international cargo trade. President Julius Maada Bio inaugurated Sierra Leone Ocean Shipping Company (SLOSCO) at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown earlier this week. The venture is 70% owned by Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with the remaining 30% held by the state-owned Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency (SLNSA). The company plans to establish a fleet of 50 ships, with an initial phase involving 30 vessels, targeting dry bulk, liquid bulk and other cargoes. Its principal markets include Sierra Leone’s substantial iron ore and bauxite exports, alongside imports of petroleum products, grain and other essential commodities. The new venture follows the restructuring of Sierra Leone’s longstanding national shipping company into SLNSA last year. Legislation provides the national carrier with rights covering 40% of the value of the country’s import and export cargoes. SLOSCO is headed by chief executive Sui Xiao, with former BRS Shipbrokers executive Laurent Debart serving as chief operating officer. The venture represents another expansion of Chinese shipping interests in West Africa, with Freetown seeking to retain more of the freight revenue generated by its international trade.

items.summary: LVR Flote, a provider of technical port services, and connectivity technology company HARDMODE have partnered to develop and test secure communications technologies for ports and the wider maritime sector as a crucial part of critical infrastructure. The Port of Riga will serve as a real-world testing environment for new connectivity solutions designed to remain reliable in challenging conditions, where connectivity is a must for mission-critical operations. The result is one solution rather than a set of systems someone has to integrate on site, and the Port of Riga is the right place to prove that in real operations.” The Baltic Sea region has experienced repeated GNSS interference affecting shipping and port operations in recent years. As a developer of dual-use connectivity solutions for defence, critical infrastructure, first responders and maritime environments, HARDMODE, together with LVR Flote, will research how different communication technologies, such as mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband, can support port operations in a single joint ecosystem. LVR Flote brings direct operational expertise and real service requirements, helping technology companies pilot new solutions for ports and the wider maritime sector in a real port environment and see how different systems work together. In return, LVR Flote gains access to solutions that could improve the efficiency, resilience and quality of port technical services.

The extent of any typhoon-induced disruption will depend on how long restrictions remain in place, the number of vessels affected and how quickly terminals can clear backlogs once operations resume. items.original_title: Intra-Asia rates soften as congestion at major ports begins to ease
items.summary: Intra-Asia rates are receding from their recent highs as bottlenecks in major Chinese and other Asian ports subside. On 15 October, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index dipped 3%, to an average of $1,453 per 40ft. Rates from Shanghai to key destinations, including Busan in South Korea, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Jawaharlal Nehru Port in India, softened as vessel waiting times declined. Rates from Shanghai to Nhava Sheva fell 11%, to $3,370 per 40ft, while those to Busan declined 8% to $1,000 per 40ft. Shanghai–Singapore rates dropped 7% to $1,973 per 40ft. Port congestion eased during Week 41, with average vessel waiting times at Busan at 23 hours, from 26 hours a week earlier. At Jawaharlal Nehru Port, waiting times declined to 24 hours, from 42, and Singapore recorded a decrease to 34 hours, from 50. However, the deteriorating situation in the Middle East continued to support freight rates on the Shanghai–Jebel Ali route, which remained elevated, at $8,416 per 40ft. Freight rates from Busan to Shanghai rose 4%, to $159 per 40ft, with Yokohama to Shanghai up 4%, to $120 per 40ft.
